metaTitle: Kodely vs Rocket.new: Which AI Builder Should You Use? (2026)
metaDescription: A factual comparison of Kodely and Rocket.new: pricing and credits, real code vs black box, hosting, backend depth, and security — so you pick the right tool.
bodyHtml:
If you're choosing between Kodely and Rocket.new, the honest answer is: it depends on what you're building. Both let you describe an app in plain English and get something working back. But they're built for different jobs — one is a focused frontend builder that hands you real, inspectable code and free hosting; the other positions itself as a broader full-stack app builder aimed at getting an idea into something usable fast. This page lays out where each one actually stands, without inflating either.

TL;DR verdict

CategoryKodelyRocket.new
OutputReal Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 codebasePositions itself as a broader full-stack app builder
See the codeYes — in-app code view of real component filesVaries by plan; check current terms before assuming

Failed buildsNever charged (one auto-repair attempt first)Varies by plan; check current terms before assuming
Free tier750 credits, no card requiredVaries by plan; check current terms before assuming

Where we couldn't verify a current Rocket.new detail with confidence, we've said so rather than guessing — their pricing and feature set change, so check their site directly before deciding on facts we haven't confirmed. Everything in the Kodely column is what the product does today.

Pricing and the credit model

Kodely gives you 750 credits free on signup, no credit card needed. After that, you top up: $9 for 500 credits, $40 for 2,500 credits (the most popular tier), or $90 for 6,000 credits. Credits don't expire. A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits, and a follow-up change is usually in the same range, so the free tier is enough to actually build and iterate on something before you have to decide whether to pay.

The detail that matters most in any credit-based builder: what happens when a generation fails. On Kodely, a build that doesn't compile is never charged — the system attempts one automatic repair first, and only successful output costs credits. This matters because charging for broken output is a real, recurring complaint across the AI-builder category generally. We don't have confirmed, current numbers on how Rocket.new prices or handles failed generations, so rather than guess, we'd point you to their own pricing page to check directly. If failed-build billing matters to you, it's worth asking them the question explicitly before you commit.

Do you actually own or see the code?

This is where the two tools diverge most clearly. Every Kodely project starts from a real foundation codebase — hand-built UI primitives like Button, Card, Section, and Nav — and every change you request edits actual .tsx component files, not a template being reconfigured behind the scenes. You can open the in-app code view at any point and see exactly what was generated. That's a meaningful trust signal: you're not being handed a black box, you're looking at a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind app as it's built.

One honest limitation: Kodely doesn't yet support exporting or downloading your project as a zip. You can view and copy the source from inside the app, but there's no one-click full-project export today. If a portable, downloadable codebase is a hard requirement for you right now, that's a real gap worth weighing.

We can't speak with certainty to whether or how Rocket.new exposes its generated code or what export options it currently offers — that's changed across builders in this category over time, so check their current documentation rather than relying on outside claims.

Hosting and going live

Kodely's publish flow is deliberately simple: one click puts your build live on a real public URL at yourname.kodely.site, free and included — there's no separate hosting decision, no extra charge, and no additional setup step. Every publish is also scanned for accidentally-leaked secrets or API keys before it goes live, which is a small but genuinely useful safety net if you're moving fast and pasting in credentials while iterating.

The tradeoff: custom domains aren't supported yet. If you need yourbrand.com rather than a kodely.site subdomain, that's not available today.

We don't have verified current details on Rocket.new's hosting model, domain support, or whether publishing is free or gated — check their pricing page for the current answer.

Backend depth — where Kodely is honest about its limits

This is the most important thing to know before you pick Kodely for a project: it generates a real frontend application only. There's no database, no authentication, no payments, and no backend generation. If your project needs user accounts, persisted data, or server-side logic, Kodely isn't the tool for that today — full stop.

Rocket.new's positioning leans toward broader full-stack output, aiming to take an idea further toward a complete, working app in one pass. If your project genuinely needs backend functionality out of the gate, that broader scope may be the more practical starting point — we're not going to pretend otherwise just because this is a Kodely page. The honest way to choose is by what you're actually building: a marketing site, portfolio, landing page, or frontend prototype fits Kodely's current scope well; an app that needs logins and a database today needs something with backend generation, whether that's Rocket.new or another tool, until Kodely adds that layer.

Security

Kodely scans every publish for leaked secrets and API keys before the site goes live, which catches a common mistake — pasting a live key into a chat prompt and having it end up in shipped code. It's a narrow but real protection, and it runs automatically with no setup on your part.

We don't have independent, verified information about Rocket.new's security scanning or review process, so we won't characterize it one way or the other. If security posture is a deciding factor for you, ask directly what checks run before a build goes live.

Best for

Pick Kodely if: you're building a marketing site, landing page, portfolio, or frontend-only product; you want to see and understand the actual code being written rather than trust a black box; you want to publish for free without a separate hosting decision; and you want a credit system where a failed build doesn't cost you anything.

Pick Rocket.new (or another full-stack builder) if: your project needs backend functionality — logins, a database, payments — from day one, and you want that generated as part of the initial build rather than added later.

The two aren't strictly interchangeable, and the right call depends on what you're shipping, not which tool markets itself louder.

FAQ

Does Kodely have a database or backend?

No. Kodely generates a real frontend application — Vite, React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS v4 — with no database, authentication, or payment generation today. If your project needs those, Kodely isn't the right fit yet.

Can I download or export my project from Kodely?

Not as a zip file. You can view and copy the actual generated source files from inside the app, but there's no full-project export or download today.

Is publishing free on Kodely?

Yes. Publishing to a yourname.kodely.site URL is free and included — there's no separate hosting cost or step.

Custom domains aren't supported yet, only *.kodely.site subdomains.

What happens if a Kodely build fails?

You're not charged. Kodely attempts one automatic repair first, and only a successful, compiling build uses credits.

Do I need a credit card to try Kodely?

No. You get 750 credits free on signup, no card required, which is typically enough for a first build and at least one round of changes.

Which is cheaper, Kodely or Rocket.new?

We can't make an honest direct comparison here — we don't have confirmed, current pricing details for Rocket.new. Kodely's pricing is straightforward: 750 free credits, then $9 for 500, $40 for 2,500, or $90 for 6,000, all non-expiring. Compare that against Rocket.new's current published pricing directly.

Can I see the actual code Kodely generates before I trust it?

Yes. Every project uses the in-app code view to show the real component files being written and edited as you chat — it's not hidden. You can sign up and check this yourself with the free credits before spending anything.

For current plan details, see pricing, or browse more comparisons and guides on the blog.

title: Kodely vs Lovable
metaTitle: Kodely vs Lovable: Which AI Builder Should You Use? (2026)
metaDescription: Kodely and Lovable both turn prompts into real code. Here's an honest comparison of pricing, code visibility, hosting, backend depth, and security in 2026.
bodyHtml:
Kodely and Lovable both let you describe a site or app in plain English and get working code back instead of a drag-and-drop mockup. That's where the similarity ends. They make different bets about what "AI builder" should mean in 2026 — one focused on full-stack apps with a database attached, the other focused on getting a real, inspectable frontend live fast without a hosting decision to make. Here's how they actually compare, without the marketing gloss on either side.

TL;DR verdict

CategoryKodelyLovable
What it buildsReal Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 frontend appFull-stack app, frontend + optional backend via Supabase
See the codeYes, in-app code view of real source filesYes, in-app code view of real source files
Download/export codeNot yet — view and copy onlyYes, GitHub sync and export
Backend / database / authNot yet — frontend onlyYes, via built-in Supabase integration
Hosting to go liveFree, one click, included on *.kodely.siteHosting included on a Lovable subdomain; custom domains typically require a paid plan
Custom domainNot yetYes, on paid plans
Pricing modelMetered credits from real generation cost; failed builds aren't chargedMetered credits/messages on subscription tiers
Free tier750 credits, no credit cardLimited free messages, no credit card
Rollback to earlier versionFree — checkpoints don't cost creditsVersion history available on the platform
Best forLanding pages, marketing sites, prototypes, portfolios you want live todayFull-stack apps that need a real database, auth, or backend logic

Pricing and the credit model

Both tools charge by usage rather than a flat "unlimited" fee, which makes sense given how expensive a single AI generation can be. The details of how you're charged matter more than the sticker price.

Kodely gives every new account 750 free credits with no credit card required. A first build typically runs 100–150 credits, and a follow-up change is usually in the same range, so the free tier covers several real iterations before you need to pay anything. When you do top up, it's straightforward: $9 for 500 credits, $40 for 2,500 credits (the most popular tier), or $90 for 6,000 credits — and credits never expire. Full pricing details are on the pricing page.

The part of Kodely's model worth calling out specifically: a build that fails to compile is never charged. Kodely runs one automatic repair attempt first, and only a successful, compiling build consumes credits. This directly addresses a complaint that's been raised repeatedly about AI builders in general — being billed for a broken output you can't use is a bad experience, and it's one Kodely designed around from the start.

Lovable also runs on a credit/message-based system layered under subscription tiers. We won't put exact current numbers on Lovable's pricing here since plans and limits change and we don't want to misquote them — check Lovable's own pricing page for the current breakdown. What we can say honestly: Lovable is a more mature, broader product, and its pricing reflects a wider feature set (backend included, team seats on higher tiers, custom domains). If you only need a frontend site, you may be paying for capability you won't use.

Do you own or see the code?

This is where both tools distinguish themselves from typical no-code builders, and where they're genuinely close. Neither Kodely nor Lovable hides your app behind a proprietary black-box format — both generate a real, readable codebase (React/TypeScript in both cases) and let you view the actual source files in-app, not an abstraction of them.

The difference is what happens after you look. Lovable supports exporting your project — syncing it to GitHub or pulling the full codebase out to run and deploy anywhere else. Kodely, today, lets you view and copy source files from the code view, but there's no zip export or GitHub sync yet. If "I need to eventually take this codebase to my own repo and deploy it myself" is a hard requirement, that's a real gap and Lovable currently covers it better. If your goal is "get a real site live and keep iterating through chat," the lack of export doesn't come up in practice — you're not leaving the platform anyway.

Neither tool currently offers click-to-edit visual editing (dragging elements, adjusting spacing with a mouse). Both are chat-first: you describe the change, the AI edits the real components, and you see the result in a live preview of the compiled app.

Hosting and going live

This is Kodely's clearest, most defensible advantage. Publishing is a single click, it's free and included — no separate hosting provider, no deploy step, no "connect your own hosting account" detour. The site goes live on a real public URL at yourname.kodely.site immediately. There's no custom domain support yet, so you're on the kodely.site subdomain for now, but for a landing page, prototype, or portfolio you want live today, that's rarely a blocker.

Lovable also gets you to a live URL quickly, and its hosting is capable enough to run full-stack apps with a working backend behind them — which is a heavier lift than a static frontend. Custom domains are supported, but generally gated behind a paid plan rather than being free on every tier. If a branded domain from day one matters to you, that's worth checking against Lovable's current plan structure.

In short: Kodely optimizes for "live in one click, no decisions." Lovable optimizes for "live with more configuration options, including your own domain, once you're paying."

Backend depth: the honest gap

This is the comparison we won't dress up. Lovable has a real, working backend story through its Supabase integration — a connected project gets a Postgres database, authentication, and server-side logic you can wire the frontend to, all inside the same chat-driven workflow. If you're building something that needs user accounts, stored data, or payments, Lovable can currently take you there.

Kodely cannot, today. What Kodely generates is a real frontend application — components, routing, styling, state — and nothing on the backend. There's no database, no authentication, and no payments generation built in. If your project needs any of those, Kodely isn't the right tool for it yet.

We're not going to pretend otherwise or bury it in a footnote: if you need a full-stack app with a database and auth right now, use Lovable. Kodely's lane today is frontend sites — marketing pages, landing pages, portfolios, product showcases, prototypes — done well and shipped fast. That's a narrower scope by design, not an oversight, and it's the honest tradeoff for a tool that gets you from prompt to a real, published site in one click without ever touching a hosting or database configuration screen.

Security

Whichever tool generates your site, publishing code you didn't hand-write comes with a specific risk: an AI model can accidentally hardcode a real API key or secret into a component, and if that ships to a public URL, it's exposed to anyone who views source. Kodely scans every publish for accidentally-leaked secrets and API keys before the site goes live, catching that class of mistake before it becomes a public incident rather than after.

Beyond that specific check, standard practice applies to either tool: review chat-generated code for anything that looks like a credential, don't paste real secrets into a prompt, and treat AI-generated code with the same scrutiny you'd give a first draft from a junior engineer — because that's functionally what it is.

Best-for verdict

  • Choose Kodely if: you need a real frontend site — landing page, portfolio, marketing site, product prototype — live on a public URL today, you want to inspect and understand the actual code being generated, and you don't want to think about hosting, deploy steps, or getting billed for a build that didn't work.
  • Choose Lovable if: your project needs a real backend — user accounts, a database, server-side logic — and you want that wired up inside the same AI workflow, or you know you'll need to export the codebase to your own repository and infrastructure.

They're not solving the identical problem, so "which is better" depends on whether you're building a site or an application. For frontend-only projects, Kodely gets you from idea to a live, free URL with fewer steps and no billing surprise on a failed build. For anything that needs a backend, Lovable is currently the more complete tool, and we'd rather tell you that directly than pretend otherwise.

You can try Kodely's 750 free credits with no credit card at signup, or log in if you already have an account. More comparisons and build breakdowns are on the blog.

FAQ

Is Kodely cheaper than Lovable?

It depends on what you're building and how you use each tool, and Lovable's current pricing tiers aren't something we'll guess at here. What we can say concretely is that Kodely never charges credits for a build that fails to compile — only a successful, working build costs you anything. That protects your credit balance from AI mistakes regardless of how the raw per-credit cost compares.

Can I use my own domain with Kodely?

Not yet. Every Kodely site publishes to a free yourname.kodely.site subdomain. Custom domain support isn't available today.

Does Kodely have a database or backend like Lovable's Supabase integration?

No. Kodely generates a real frontend application only — no database, authentication, or payments today. If your project needs a backend, Lovable's Supabase integration currently covers that and Kodely doesn't.

Can I download or export the code Kodely generates?

Not yet. You can view and copy the actual source files from Kodely's in-app code view, but there's no zip download or GitHub export at this time. Lovable does support exporting your project.

What happens if a generation fails on Kodely?

Kodely automatically attempts one repair before giving up. If the build still doesn't compile, you're not charged credits for it — you only pay for builds that actually work.

Is my generated site checked for security issues before it goes live?

Yes. Every Kodely publish is scanned for accidentally-leaked secrets or API keys before the site becomes publicly accessible.

Can I roll back to an earlier version of my site?

Yes. Every successful generation in Kodely creates a checkpoint, and rolling back to an earlier one is free — it's not treated as a new generation and doesn't cost credits.

title: Build a Booking or Appointment Website with AI
metaTitle: How to Build a Booking/Appointment Website with AI (No Code Needed)
metaDescription: Build a real booking or appointment website with AI in one prompt. See exactly what Kodely generates, what's UI-only today, and how to publish it live for free.
targetKeyword: build a booking appointment website with AI
bodyHtml:
What a good booking or appointment site actually needs

Before you generate anything, it helps to know what "good" looks like for this category of site. A booking or appointment page that actually converts visitors into customers usually has the same handful of ingredients, whether it's for a massage therapist, a dog groomer, or a two-person law firm:

  • A clear list of services with prices or price ranges, so people aren't guessing
  • A request-an-appointment form that asks for the right details up front (service, preferred date/time, contact info, notes)
  • Hours and location, visible without scrolling to the footer
  • Social proof — a few real-sounding testimonials or a review count
  • A strong, specific call to action ("Request an Appointment," not "Submit")

None of that requires a database on day one. It requires good copy, a clean layout, and a form that looks and feels trustworthy. That's exactly the part AI is good at generating quickly — and it's where Kodely starts.

The one-prompt approach

You don't need a spec document or a Figma file. You need one well-written prompt that tells Kodely three things: who the business is, what makes it specific (not generic), and what you want on the page. Vague prompts produce vague sites — "make me a booking website" gives Kodely almost nothing to work with. The fix isn't a longer conversation, it's a more specific first message.

Name the business. Name the services. Name the vibe. That's it.

Example prompt

Here's a real prompt you can copy, edit with your own business details, and paste straight into Kodely:

"Build a booking website for 'Riverbend Massage & Wellness,' a massage therapy studio in Portland. Services: 60-minute Swedish massage ($95), 90-minute deep tissue ($140), and a couples massage package ($220). Warm, calming design — sage green and cream, soft rounded cards, no harsh colors. Include a hero section with a headline and a 'Request an Appointment' button, a services section with the three options above, an appointment request form (name, email, phone, preferred service, preferred date, notes), an hours & location section (Tue–Sat, 10am–6pm, 442 Hawthorne Blvd), and three short client testimonials."

Notice what's doing the work: a real business name, real service names and prices, a specific color direction, and an explicit list of sections. Kodely can fill in reasonable defaults if you leave things out, but every specific detail you give it is one less thing you'll have to fix afterward.

What Kodely generates — and what's UI-only for now

When you send that prompt, Kodely builds a real Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 app — actual component files, not an HTML template and not a static mockup. It starts from a foundation codebase with hand-built UI primitives (buttons, cards, sections, nav), so the result looks like a designed product from the first generation, not a rough draft. You'll see it come together in a live preview as it builds.

For a booking site specifically, here's what that gets you, and where the honest line sits today:

  • What you get: a genuinely good-looking, fully responsive booking page — services list, pricing, an appointment request form with proper fields and validation-style UI, hours and location, testimonials, and a working navigation and layout. It reads and behaves like a real booking flow.
  • What you don't get yet: a backend. There's no database behind the form, so a submitted appointment request doesn't get saved anywhere and no email or SMS notification goes out. The form is real UI — real inputs, real client-side behavior — but submissions aren't persisted or delivered yet. Wiring a form to actually save appointments and notify the business is coming in a future release, and it's the natural next step once you've got the front end looking right.

If you're using this to pitch a client, mock up a redesign, or get a real business online with a professional first impression while you sort out how bookings will actually be handled (a phone number, an email link, or a scheduling tool embedded later), this gets you most of the way there today. If you need customers booking real appointments into a real calendar right now, that piece isn't built yet — don't promise it to a client until it is.

Customizing it through chat

Once the first version is generated, everything after that is a conversation, not a rebuild. You don't touch code or hunt through a settings panel — you just describe the change:

  • "Add a fourth service: hot stone massage, 75 minutes, $155"
  • "Make the hero section full-width with a background image instead of a solid color"
  • "Change the testimonials to a 3-column grid on desktop and stack them on mobile"
  • "Add a FAQ section above the footer with questions about cancellation policy and what to wear"

Kodely edits the real component files behind the scenes, and you see the result in the live preview. If a generation doesn't compile, Kodely attempts one automatic repair before it ever charges you for it. And because every successful generation is saved as a checkpoint, if a change makes things worse, rolling back to the previous version is free — it's not treated as a new generation, so it doesn't cost you anything to undo a bad direction. You can also open the code view at any point to see and copy the actual generated source files.

Publishing it live

When the page looks right, publishing is one click. Kodely puts it on a real public URL at <yourname>.kodely.site — free, included, with no separate hosting step to configure. Every publish is automatically scanned for accidentally-leaked secrets or API keys before it goes live, so you're not shipping something you'll regret. From there, you can keep iterating in chat and republish as often as you want.

A couple of things worth knowing before you publish: today, sites live on a kodely.site subdomain — there's no custom domain support yet — and there's no zip or full-project download, so if you need to hand the code to another developer or hosting platform, that export path isn't available right now. You can still view and copy individual source files from the in-app code view.

FAQ

Can Kodely build a booking site that actually saves appointments to a database?

Not yet. Kodely generates a real, polished frontend — including a fully-designed appointment request form — but there's no backend, database, or notification system behind it today. The form looks and behaves like a working booking flow; it just doesn't persist submissions yet. That's on the roadmap.

How much does it cost to build a booking site this way?

Credits are metered from real AI cost, not a flat per-project fee. A first build like the Riverbend example above typically runs somewhere in the 100–150 credit range, and a follow-up change is usually similar. You get 750 credits free on signup with no credit card required, which is normally enough to build and refine a site like this several times over. If you need more, top-ups start at $9 for 500 credits, and credits never expire. See pricing for the full breakdown.

Do I need to know how to code?

No. You describe what you want in plain English and Kodely generates the actual code for you. If you do know how to code, or want to learn from what's generated, the in-app code view shows you the real component files.

Can I use my own domain instead of kodely.site?

Not yet — custom domains aren't supported today. Every published site gets a free subdomain at <yourname>.kodely.site.

What if I don't like how the first version turns out?

Keep talking to it. Describe exactly what's wrong — "the services section feels cramped, add more spacing" or "this color scheme doesn't match a wellness studio, try something softer" — and Kodely regenerates the relevant components. Every successful version is checkpointed, so you can roll back for free if a change doesn't work out.

Is this good enough to show a real client?

For the visual design, layout, copy, and overall first impression — yes, that's exactly what it's built for. Just be upfront that the appointment form doesn't save data yet if that matters for how the client plans to use it. Being honest about that now is a lot better than a client finding out the hard way later.

Ready to try it? Create a free account and generate your first booking site with 750 free credits — no credit card required.

bodyHtml:
What a good product showcase site actually needs

Before you touch any tool, it helps to separate two things people lump together under "online store": the storefront and the checkout system.

The storefront is everything a shopper sees and browses: a homepage that sells the brand, a product grid, individual product pages with photos and descriptions, and a clear way to take the next step. The checkout system is the plumbing behind it: a product database, a cart that persists across pages, payment processing, order records, inventory, and (usually) an account system. Building a real checkout system is a serious backend project on its own, independent of how good the design looks.

Most small brands, makers, and service businesses don't actually need the second part on day one. What they need is a storefront that looks credible enough to convert visitors into inquiries, calls, DMs, or emails — while they sell through Instagram checkout, a marketplace, in person, or a simple "email us to order" flow. That's the gap Kodely is built to fill today.

The one-prompt approach

Instead of wireframing pages, picking a theme, and configuring plugins, you open Kodely and describe the store in plain English: who it's for, what you sell, and the mood you want. Kodely reads that description and generates a real Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 app — not a template with placeholder text, and not a static mockup. Every project starts from a hand-built foundation codebase (real Button, Card, Section, and Nav components), so the first generation is already a working, styled app rather than a blank canvas.

You watch the live preview render as it's built. If something's off — wrong tone, wrong layout, missing a section — you say so in chat and Kodely edits the actual component files, the same way a developer would.

Example prompt (copy this and adapt it)

Vague prompts get vague stores. The more specific you are about products, price points, and voice, the closer the first generation lands. Here's a real prompt for a small handmade-goods brand:

"Build a storefront for Ember & Oak, a small-batch candle studio in Portland. Warm, minimal, editorial feel — think earthy neutrals, not neon. Homepage needs a hero with our tagline 'Hand-poured, one batch at a time,' a featured-products row, and a short brand story section. Product grid page showing these 6 candles: Cedar Smoke ($28), Fig & Vetiver ($28), Amber Dusk ($32), Sea Salt Driftwood ($28), Vanilla Bourbon ($32), and Bergamot Moss ($28) — each with a short one-line scent description. Each product needs its own detail page with a larger image area, the price, scent notes, burn time, and an 'Inquire to Order' button that opens a contact form instead of a cart, since we take orders by email for now. Add a simple About page and a footer with Instagram and email contact."

Notice what that prompt does: it names real products and prices, describes the visual mood instead of just saying "make it nice," and is explicit that ordering happens through an inquiry form, not a cart. That honesty in the prompt is what keeps the output honest too.

What Kodely generates today (showcase, not checkout)

Be clear-eyed about this before you start: Kodely will build you a genuinely good-looking, real-code storefront — a homepage, a product grid, individual product detail layouts, and a contact or "inquire to order" flow. What it will not do, today, is generate a working cart, payment processing, or order database. There's no backend, no database, and no payments layer yet.

That makes Kodely the right tool for:

  • A catalog site for a brand that takes orders by email, DM, phone, or in person
  • A "coming soon" or pre-launch storefront while you set up real payments elsewhere
  • A lookbook-style site that drives traffic to an existing marketplace listing or Instagram shop
  • A client pitch or portfolio piece that needs to look like a real store fast

It is not yet the right tool for a self-serve checkout where a stranger can land on the site, add items to a cart, and pay on the spot. If that's what you need right now, Kodely can still get you the entire visual storefront in minutes — you'd just wire a checkout provider in separately, which isn't something Kodely does for you today.

Every generation is also a checkpoint. If a follow-up change goes somewhere you didn't want, you roll back to the previous version for free — it's a restore, not a new build, so it doesn't cost credits. And if a generation fails to compile, Kodely attempts one automatic repair before it ever charges you.

Customizing it through chat

Once the first version exists, refine it the same way you built it — by describing the change. For a storefront, typical follow-ups look like:

  • "Make the product cards bigger and add a hover effect that shows the scent notes"
  • "Add a 'Best Seller' badge to Amber Dusk and Vanilla Bourbon"
  • "Change the color palette to be darker and more moody, less beige"
  • "Add an FAQ section above the footer covering shipping time and returns"
  • "Swap the 'Inquire to Order' button copy to 'Email to Order This Scent'"

Each request edits the real component files — you can open code view at any point and see (and copy) the actual source. Short definition

Vibe coding is a way of building software where you describe what you want in plain, everyday language and an AI writes and iterates the actual code for you. Instead of typing out functions and markup line by line, you stay in a conversation: you say what you want to see or happen, the AI produces working code, you look at the result, and you ask for changes until it matches what's in your head. The "coding" still happens — it's just that the AI is the one typing.

Where the term comes from

"Vibe coding" was popularized in early 2025 by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who used it to describe a loose, conversational style of building with AI coding assistants: you describe the vibe of what you want, let the model generate the implementation, and steer by reacting to what comes back rather than reading every line. The phrase caught on fast because it named something a lot of people were already doing — using chat-based AI tools to build real software without treating every keystroke as sacred. By 2026 it's become the common shorthand for natural-language, AI-driven development in general, including tools built specifically for websites and apps.

A plain-language analogy

Think about the difference between building furniture by hand and describing what you want to a skilled carpenter. Traditional coding is like being the carpenter yourself: you cut every board, measure every joint, and if something's off, you go back and re-cut it. Vibe coding is more like telling that carpenter, "I want a bookshelf, about this wide, with a closed cabinet at the bottom, in a warm wood tone" — then looking at what they build, and saying "make the shelves a bit deeper" or "add a door there instead." You're not doing the joinery. You're directing the outcome, in your own words, and reacting to what shows up.

Why it matters

Vibe coding matters because it moves the bottleneck of building software from knowing how to write code to knowing what you want. That opens the door to a much wider set of people:

  • Non-developers — small business owners, marketers, designers, students — can produce real, working software without first learning a programming language.

It's not that code stops mattering — real code is still being written and run. What changes is who can direct that code getting written, and how quickly.
